text: People go to school for 25 years and
have very little wisdom to show for it.
That's because wisdom requires a certain
type of work, work that most either
don't know to do or aren't willing to
do.
As Ryan Holiday explains in his new
book, it's not enough to learn new
ideas. You need to interrogate them for
value, connect them to what you already
know, and apply them to your life.
Then, after some time, you need to
reflect on their usefulness.
But this takes time and energy that most
of us simply don't invest.
But what good is wisdom anyway?
Why bother putting in the work?
Wisdom is worth the work because it
plants the seeds of personal freedom.
Wisdom gives you a deep understanding of
yourself and the human condition,
helping you let go of the destructive
habits that trap most people, like the
hedonic treadmill or the comparison
trap.
It helps you navigate the internal
forces trying to hold you back,
especially self-sabotage in the form of
procrastination.
Wisdom also frees you from unnecessary
anxiety, worry, and chronic stress by
allowing you to realize that this too
shall pass and that you need less than
you think to be happy.
That's why as people grow older and
wiser, they often become happier despite
their declining health.
Earn the freedom that wisdom provides by
putting in the work in three distinct
ways starting today.
First, work with what you read.
Read more books.
Even in the age of AI, books offer
something unique.
Books contain years of lived experience,
carefully refined, and take years to
thoughtfully put together.
Put simply, writing a good book requires
refined judgment. And what is wisdom if
not exactly that?
So, here's my challenge to you. Starting
tomorrow, trade half your phone and TV
time for reading great books.
Focus on three book categories.
First, read about the human condition.
Start with The Diary of Anne Frank, The
Gulag Archipelago by Aleksandr
Solzhenitsyn, and When Breath Becomes
Air by Paul Kalanithi.
These books showcase the remarkable
strength people can summon in the
darkest of circumstances.
Second, read timeless philosophical
books that present different approaches
to living.
Pick up Meditations by Marcus Aurelius,
The Bhagavad Gita, or Walden by Henry
David Thoreau.
Each provides a distinct perspective on
living meaningfully.
Third, explore books that deepen
self-knowledge. Books like The
Untethered Soul by Michael A. Singer,
Man's Search for Meaning by Viktor E.
Frankl, and Awareness by Anthony de
Mello.
Now, if you simply flip through the
pages of those books, you failed.
What separates casual readers from truly
wise ones can be summed up in one word,
extraction.
You must deliberately extract what
matters.
Here's how Ryan Holiday does it.
As he reads, he makes notes in the
margins.
Then, after finishing a book, he waits 1
to 2 weeks before reviewing his notes.
This delay is crucial because it filters
out ideas that would have little impact
on his life or work.
He extracts only the most memorable
insights onto 4 by 6 index cards.
One idea per card.
A great book might yield 20 to 30 cards.
Now, you might prefer a digital notes
system like Notion or Obsidian, and
that's okay. Just ensure you have one
idea per note.
Ryan Holiday's note cards include three
things, the idea itself as a direct
quote or short summary, the theme that
connects it to other ideas, like
Stoicism or apprenticeship, and a
personal note on why it matters and how
he might use it.
Now, if you follow a similar method of
extraction, you'll burn useful ideas
into your mind and begin applying them
in your life.
The next way you must work to be wiser
is to work to see your thinking.
In December 1941, just days after the
attack on Pearl Harbor, Japan was
rapidly taking the Philippines and other
Pacific Islands, and the United States
now had to fight a two-front war with
supply lines that stretched thousands of
miles.
The US Army's Chief of Staff, George
Marshall, called in General Dwight D.
Eisenhower into his office and asked,
"What should our approach be?"
Most officers would have started
brainstorming aloud, but Eisenhower
said, "Give me a few hours."
He found a desk in the war plans
division, grabbed some paper, and
started writing.
After pouring his ideas onto the page,
he'd pause and push himself.
Are these risks worth taking?
What are the trade-offs? What am I
missing?
Like Eisenhower, wise people aren't
afraid to ask for time to get their
thinking straight, even when the
pressure is intense.
And to get their thinking right, they
know they must write.
Writing out your thoughts allows you to
see them clearly and spot flaws, biases,
or gaps in logic.
Joan Didion once said, "I don't know
what I think until I write it down."
Writing for her was an exploration, a
way to discover what her mind truly held
once it hit the page.
Whenever possible, work to understand
what you think on a topic before you
open your mouth.
The third way you can work to be wise is
to work to be wrong.
Most people use AI to be proven right.
AI chatbots know this, so they're quick
to affirm whatever ideas you throw at
them.
Earlier this year, I heard a story on
The Daily podcast about a man who became
convinced by ChatGPT that he was on the
verge of the greatest mathematical proof
the world had ever seen.
He wasn't a mathematician, so he showed
his friends the chat history to see what
they thought.
"It seems promising," they said.
Encouraged, he emailed his AI-assisted
work to mathematicians around the world.
Not a single one responded.
After several weeks, he did something he
should have done from the start. He
asked another AI chatbot if he might be
wrong.
In seconds, the other chatbot shattered
his illusion and saved him years of
chasing a dead end.
Use AI different than most people and
actively push it to point out what's
wrong with your approach.
This could be a career path you've been
on for years, a business strategy you
haven't stopped to rethink, or an
assumption you've never challenged.
Develop thick skin and learn to take
criticism without being demoralized.
Those who cannot admit they're wrong can
never become wiser.
In the end,
pursuing wisdom is a lot like walking
toward the horizon.
You never reach it, but you periodically
look back and see how far you've
traveled.
The further you go, the calmer, more
curious, and happier you'll be.
As Epictetus said, "Wisdom is getting in
fewer fights, letting more things go,
and focusing more on what you control."
That was the core message that I
gathered from Wisdom Takes Work by Ryan
Holiday.
